before.title: 1G ECU Electrolytic Capacitor Leakage (Rough Idle, No-Start)
before.description: The electrolytic capacitors in 1990-1994 ECUs have defective seals and leak electrolyte onto the circuit board, corroding traces and surface-mount components — 1990-1993 units are worst, and the front capacitor in 1990 ECUs is known to short and burn through the board under it, taking out the idle speed control circuit. Symptoms range from hunting/rough idle and hard starting to intermittent stalling and complete no-starts. The leaked electrolyte keeps eating the board over time, so an untouched 30-year-old ECU is assumed to need this repair.
before.solution: Have the ECU recapped: replace all electrolytic capacitors, neutralize and clean the electrolyte residue, and repair any damaged traces (especially the ISC traces). Specialist shops such as ECMTuning offer this service; capable DIYers can do it with basic soldering equipment.
symptoms: Rough, hunting, or surging idle
Hard starting or intermittent no-start
Random stalling
Idle speed control stops working
Visible brown residue or fishy smell on the ECU board

before.title: 2G Fuel Pump Wiring Voltage Drop and Fuel Pump/MFI Relay Failure
before.description: On 1995-1999 cars the fuel pump's factory wiring is undersized and its chassis ground (at the floor crossmember under the driver's seat) corrodes with age, dropping voltage at the pump into the 10-11V range under load. The paired fuel pump/MFI relay behind the center console can also fail. The result is intermittent cranking no-starts (no pump prime), stalling, and lean stumble or fuel cut at wide-open throttle on turbo cars — a problem so common the community-standard fix is the documented 'fuel pump rewire.'
before.solution: Test voltage at the pump and the fuel pump/MFI relay first; replace the relay if it fails continuity testing, and repair or supplement the corroded ground wire. The accepted long-term fix is the DSM fuel pump rewire: a relay-triggered, fused 12-gauge feed direct from the battery/alternator with a fresh chassis ground.
symptoms: Engine cranks but fuel pump never hums
Intermittent no-start, often after heat soak
Stalling or dying while driving
Lean stumble or fuel cut at wide-open throttle
Fuel pressure/voltage at the pump drops under load

before.title: 4G63 7-Bolt Crank Walk (Thrust Bearing Failure)
before.description: The 1995-1999 Eclipse GS-T and GSX use the 7-bolt 4G63 turbo engine, which is notoriously prone to 'crank walk' — excessive axial movement of the crankshaft caused by thrust bearing failure. The crankshaft literally moves fore-and-aft inside the block, eventually destroying the crank position sensor backplate and ruining the crank, block, and bearings. Root causes include factory-misadjusted clutch hydraulics leaving residual pressure on the thrust bearing, 7-bolt oil squirter design that bleeds pressure from main bearing feeds, and a metallurgically weaker crank than the earlier 6-bolt motor. Crankwalk was most prevalent in engines built in 1995, and most affected units failed at low mileage before the first timing belt service. There is no recall, and full repair requires a complete engine teardown with crank and bearing replacement.
before.solution: Confirm with a dial indicator on the crank snout while a helper presses the clutch (>0.010" axial movement = crank walk). The only durable fix is to pull the engine, replace the crankshaft, all main/rod/thrust bearings, and ideally install ARP main studs with dowels. Mitigation while diagnosing: verify clutch master/slave cylinder adjustment so there is zero residual pressure on the throwout bearing at rest, and disable the clutch interlock switch so drivers do not rest a foot on the clutch. Plugging the 7-bolt piston oil squirters is a common preventive modification during a rebuild.
symptoms: Ticking or clicking noise from timing belt / crank pulley area
Clutch engagement/disengagement point changes (especially on left turns)
Clutch pedal sticks down or feels inconsistent
Engine stalls or briefly cuts out when clutch is held in
Repeated crank position sensor (CKP) failures
Visible fore/aft movement of crankshaft pulley when clutch is operated

before.title: 4G63 "Crankwalk" - Crankshaft Thrust Bearing Failure (7-bolt engines)
before.description: The 1996-1999 second-generation Eclipse turbo (GS-T/GSX) uses the 7-bolt 4G63T, which is notorious for "crankwalk": the crankshaft thrust bearing wears out and allows the crank to move excessively fore-aft (lateral end-play). Marginal oiling to the thrust surface, dirt contamination, and heavy-duty clutch pressure loads accelerate the wear. As the crank walks it destroys the crankshaft position/timing signal and eventually the crankshaft itself. It is one of the most feared failures in the DSM community and is largely non-repairable without pulling the engine. The earlier 1990-1994 1G and 1995 6-bolt engines are far less prone; Mitsubishi revised the thrust bearing design (culminating in a 4-piece self-aligning thrust bearing by 1999) to mitigate it, but 1996-early-1997 cars remain high-risk.
before.solution: There is no reliable in-car fix. Diagnosis is by measuring crankshaft end-play with a dial indicator (spec is roughly 0.002-0.010 in; more than that indicates walk). Once diagnosed, the remedy is an engine rebuild or replacement with a machined/align-honed block and new thrust bearings, ideally converting to a stronger 6-bolt crank/block or using an updated split thrust bearing. Owners reduce risk with frequent oil changes, avoiding overly aggressive clutches, and not launching the car hard.
symptoms: Ticking or knocking from the timing/pulley side of the engine
Erratic idle or stalling as the crank/cam timing signal is disrupted
No-start or intermittent start
Visible fore-aft movement of the crank pulley
Fluctuating ignition timing on a light

before.title: AWD (GSX) Transfer Case Lockup - NHTSA Recall 98V069000
before.description: The all-wheel-drive Eclipse GSX was recalled (NHTSA campaign 98V069, March 1998) covering 1990-1998 GSX models. A brass plug in the center of the transfer case yoke can leak, causing insufficient lubrication in the transfer case; the transfer case can then lock up, which can cause loss of vehicle control and a crash. Roughly 24,275 vehicles were covered. Beyond the recall itself, the AWD driveline (transfer case, center differential, rear diff, and pressed-in rear wheel bearings) is a known wear area on these cars, especially if fluids were neglected.
before.solution: Under the original recall, dealers inspected transfer case oil volume, checked for leakage at the yoke plug, and inspected for operational degradation, repairing as needed at no charge. On a used car today, verify the recall was performed, keep the transfer case and differential fluids fresh (gear oil per spec), and address any yoke/output-seal leaks promptly. A failed transfer case requires rebuild or replacement; worn rear AWD wheel bearings are pressed and typically replaced as a bearing or complete hub.
symptoms: Binding, grinding, or lockup from the transfer case
Whining or howling from the driveline
Gear oil leak at the transfer case yoke/output
Vibration or driveline shudder
Rear wheel bearing growl/rumble that changes with speed

before.title: AWD Transfer Case Lockup and Output Shaft Seal Leaks (GSX, NHTSA Recall 98V069001)
before.description: On AWD GSX (and Talon TSi AWD platform) cars, the transfer case output shaft seal leaks gear oil until the case runs dry, and per NHTSA recall 98V069001 'lockup of the transfer case can occur due to insufficient lubrication.' Owners have reported the wheels locking at 50-68 mph, spinning the car, with metal shavings found inside the case; NHTSA complaint records include at least one crash. Failures and re-failures are documented from roughly 55,000 to over 200,000 miles, including on cars that already received the recall repair.
before.solution: Check the transfer case oil level and the output/yoke seal for leaks at every oil change, and reseal or replace the transfer case at the first sign of weeping. The original recall remedy was inspection, topping off, reseal, or full transfer case replacement — AWD owners should verify the recall was performed and still treat any leak as urgent.
symptoms: Gear oil leak/wet film under the transfer case
Whine or grinding from the center of the car that grows with speed
Driveline vibration at highway speed
Jerking or shaking followed by sudden wheel lockup
Metal shavings in the transfer case fluid

before.title: Balance Shaft Belt Failure Destroying the Timing Belt (Interference 4G63)
before.description: The turbo 4G63 is an interference engine, and its narrow balance shaft belt runs directly alongside the main timing belt. When the aging balance shaft belt frays or snaps — common on neglected 1G six-bolt and 2G seven-bolt cars — the debris gets caught in the timing belt, causing it to jump teeth or break outright. Because the pistons and valves share the same space, the result is at least eight bent valves and a cylinder head rebuild, and the DSM community treats overdue belts as the single most engine-destroying maintenance lapse on these cars.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt, balance shaft belt, tensioners, and idlers together every 60,000 miles, never leaving an old balance shaft belt in place behind a new timing belt. Many owners permanently remove the balance shafts with a balance shaft elimination kit (stub shaft) so the failure-prone belt is deleted entirely.
symptoms: Sudden stall while driving or idling
Engine cranks freely but will not restart
Flapping or slapping noise from the front timing cover
Visible fraying or missing teeth on belts behind the timing cover
Low oil pressure if the oil pump/balance shaft drive is disturbed

before.title: Cam Angle Sensor (CAS) / Optical Distributor Failure - No-Start and Stalling
before.description: The 4G63 uses a cam angle sensor (an optical sensor mounted in the distributor housing on the exhaust cam) to provide the crank/cam timing signal to the ECU. With age the CAS optical disc, LEDs/phototransistors, and internal bearing wear out and produce erratic or lost signals. On 1G cars the CAS is base-timing adjustable; on 2G it is fixed. Failure is a classic cause of intermittent no-start, hot-soak no-start, and random stalling on these cars, and it can be intermittent enough that tapping the sensor temporarily restores it. It is frequently misdiagnosed. (Note: crankwalk can mimic these symptoms by physically disturbing the CAS drive.)
before.solution: Diagnose by checking for spark and injector pulse and verifying the CAS output signal on a scope/meter; a bearing that has play or a signal that cuts out when hot confirms it. Replace the cam angle sensor (or the complete optical distributor assembly). On 1G cars, re-set base ignition timing after replacement. Ensure grounds and the connector are clean, as poor grounds mimic CAS faults.
symptoms: Intermittent no-start / crank but no spark
Hot-start failure (won't restart until it cools)
Random stalling while driving
Rough running that comes and goes
Symptoms temporarily clear when the sensor is tapped

before.title: Front Lower Ball Joint Boot Damage and Separation (NHTSA Recalls 99V066001 / 00V421001)
before.description: Mitsubishi issued two recalls (99V066001, then the expanded 00V421001) on 2G Eclipses because the rubber boots on the front lower lateral arm ball joints were damaged during assembly, letting dirt and water into the joint. A worn, contaminated ball joint can separate from the knuckle, dropping the front corner and causing loss of steering control. On unrepaired or high-mileage cars the same wear pattern shows up today as clunking and torn boots.
before.solution: Inspect the lower ball joint boots and check the joints for play; replace the lower lateral arm/ball joint assembly if the boot is torn or the joint has any looseness. The recall remedy was inspection, replacement of worn joints, and sealing of undamaged ones — owners of survivors should simply replace worn joints outright.
symptoms: Clunking from the front end over bumps
Torn or greasy lower ball joint boot

before.title: Front Subframe / Crossmember and Rocker Rust Corrosion (salt-belt cars)
before.description: Like most DSM-era cars, 1990s Eclipses in road-salt regions suffer structural corrosion of the front crossmember/subframe (which locates the lower control arms) as well as the rocker panels, strut towers, and rear subframe/trailing-arm mounts. Because the lower control arms bolt to the front crossmember, severe perforation can allow a control arm to loosen or detach, causing loss of control - the same failure mode Mitsubishi later addressed with formal crossmember-corrosion recalls on newer models (the cited bulletin/recall covers other Mitsubishi models and is referenced here as an analogous failure mode). On these 25-35 year-old cars it is a safety and roadworthiness concern rather than a warranty item, and heavily rusted examples are common in the Northeast/Midwest.
before.solution: Inspect the crossmember, control-arm mounts, subframe, and rockers for perforation, using a punch/hammer test on suspect areas (perforation means replacement). Repair options are welding in new steel/reinforcement plates by a competent shop or replacing the crossmember/subframe with a sound used or reproduction unit. Undercoating and keeping drains clear slows further corrosion. Do not drive a car with a perforated control-arm mount.
symptoms: Visible rust perforation of the front crossmember or control-arm mounts
Clunking or loose feel from the front suspension
Rust-through in rockers, strut towers, and rear subframe mounts
Alignment that won't hold
Flaking/soft metal that fails a punch test

before.title: Lifter Tick from Hydraulic Lash Adjusters
before.description: The 4G63's hydraulic lash adjusters (lifters) are notorious for clogging with oil varnish or bleeding down, producing the infamous DSM 'lifter tick' from the valve cover. The early-design lifters used in 1G cars were revised twice by Mitsubishi specifically to address the noise. Forum consensus is that the tick itself rarely damages the engine — many owners drive with it for years — but it is loud, persistent, and frequently mistaken for rod knock or other serious problems.
before.solution: Start with a fresh oil change at the correct viscosity; if the tick persists, remove and clean the lash adjusters or replace them with the revised Mitsubishi parts (MD337687/MD377054) or current aftermarket equivalents. New lifters must be bled before installation, and may need 20-30 minutes of running to quiet down fully.
symptoms: Rhythmic ticking/tapping from the top of the engine
Noise loudest at cold start
Tick speeds up with engine RPM
Noise changes with oil brand, weight, or oil age
Tick persists after engine is fully warm

before.title: Rust at Rear Wheel Arches, Lower Quarter Panels, and Rockers
before.description: Both 1G and 2G Eclipse/Talon bodies rot in predictable places: the rear wheel arches and the lower quarter panel just ahead of the rear tires, the rocker/support area under the doors, and — most structurally serious — the front strut towers. The arch and rocker seams trap road salt and moisture between panel layers, so by the time paint bubbles appear the rust has usually perforated multiple layers from the inside out. Forum consensus treats the rear lower wheel wells and strut towers as the first places to inspect on any survivor car.
before.solution: Cut out perforated metal and weld in patch panels or replacement quarter/arch sections, then seam-seal and rustproof the cavities; surface treatment alone does not stop inside-out rot. Eclipse and Talon steel body panels of the same generation interchange, which widens the supply of donor sheet metal. Strut tower rust requires professional structural repair.
symptoms: Bubbling paint on the rear wheel arch lips
Holes in the lower quarter panels ahead of the rear tires
Crusty or perforated rocker panels under the doors
Rust flakes or perforation around the front strut towers
Rust where the rear quarter meets the bumper cover

before.title: Timing Belt Failure on Interference 4G63 (catastrophic valve damage)
before.description: The DOHC 4G63 (both the naturally aspirated 4G63 and turbo 4G63T across 1990-1999) is an interference engine: if the timing belt snaps or jumps, the pistons strike the open valves, bending valves and often damaging the head and pistons. These belts were specified for replacement around 60,000 miles, and on 30-year-old cars many have been neglected or the balance-shaft belt has been ignored. The 4G63 also drives the oil pump off a balance shaft, so a failed balance-shaft belt can wrap around and knock the timing belt off, causing the same catastrophic result. This is the single most important preventive-maintenance item on any 1990s Eclipse.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, idler pulley, and water pump as a set every 60k miles (or on any car of unknown history). Replace the balance-shaft belt at the same time or perform a balance-shaft delete done correctly (retaining oil-pump drive) per accepted DSM practice. If a belt has already failed, repair requires removing the head for a valve job (new/straightened valves, guides, seals, machining) and inspecting the pistons - frequently 4-8 bent intake valves are found.
symptoms: Sudden loss of power / engine dies while driving and will not restart
Engine cranks but does not fire
No compression on cranking
Rattling or slapping noise before failure from a worn belt/tensioner
Resistance when turning the crank by hand (valves contacting pistons)

before.title: Valve Stem Seals Hardening - Oil Consumption and Blue Smoke at Idle
before.description: As the 4G63/4G63T ages, the valve stem seals harden and shrink, letting oil seep down the valve guides into the combustion chamber. The signature symptom is a puff of blue smoke on startup or on a quick rev after the engine has idled for a while, plus gradual oil consumption. Turbo cars can also show smoke that is confused with turbo seal failure, so proper diagnosis matters. This is a wear/age issue rather than a design defect and is very common on high-mileage 1G and 2G cars.
before.solution: Confirm the source (valve seals vs. turbo seals vs. worn rings) with a leak-down/compression test and by watching when the smoke appears. Replace the intake and exhaust valve stem seals; on the 4G63 this can be done with the head on the engine using a valve-spring compressor and compressed air to hold the valves, which greatly reduces labor. If oil control rings or guides are also worn, a head rebuild is required.
symptoms: Blue smoke on cold startup
Puff of smoke when revving after idling
Gradual oil consumption between changes
Oil fouling of spark plugs
Smoke on deceleration/overrun
